# Introduction

In an era characterised by globalisation and increasing interconnectedness, proﬁciency in additional languages, even extending beyond just a second language (L2), has emerged as a critical asset for university students’ career development across various industries and professions. This is particularly prominent in developing countries, including Türkiye, especially given the upward trajectory of youth unemployment rates (Taş et al., 2018), coupled with the growing annual influx of graduate students (Adıgüzel, [2021)](#disclosure-statement). In this scenario, the English language, recognised as the global lingua franca (Crystal, 2003) and the international language for business (Bloch, 1995), carries considerable signiﬁcance in Türkiye, where it is taught as a foreign language (EFL). Acknowledging this, edu- cational policies in Türkiye have long mandated the inclusion of English in the centralised curricu- lum, starting from the second grade in primary schools through the ﬁrst year of tertiary education. Currently, this asset, that is, L2 proﬁciency, eases university enrolment and graduation for particular programmes, serves as a requirement for pursuing academic studies and international education, and, predictably, guarantees qualiﬁcation for job opportunities and career advancement in both public and private sectors. In this respect, the following statement would likely be elucidat- ing and still relevant: “A foreign language is not an open ticket to the position of one’s dreams, but

the message from the growing number of businesses looking abroad is that a graduate with language skills, particularly one with a measure of professional training, is at a deﬁnite advantage” (Financial Times, 1990, p. 43)

The signiﬁcance of proﬁciency in L2, a fundamental requirement for entering the workforce (Bíre- šová, 2009), has been furthered in the European Commission’s multilingual policy aimed at fostering a functional multilingual economy (Hrehova, 2010). Moreover, several studies elaborated on this matter of concern. For example, Sindik and Božinović (2013) reported the importance of the mastery of foreign languages for a career in the tourism sector in Croatia, while Shrestha et al. (2015) emphasised the merit of L2 English proﬁciency for the career prospects of Nepalese engineer- ing students. Additionally, Peltokorpi (2023) presented evidence supporting the direct correlation between L2 English proﬁciency and job promotions, salary increases, and career satisfaction in the Japanese context. Along similar lines, Pudelko and Tenzer (2019) uncovered both direct and indirect effects of language barriers as an impediment to global career opportunities in international business schools across four countries. Finally, Miranda and Umhoefer (1998) identiﬁed L2 English proﬁciency and acculturation as predictors of career self-efficacy among Latino individuals in the United States.

L2 proﬁciency, therefore, can be regarded as a necessary attribute that expands both domestic and international career opportunities. It provides individuals with access to global work contexts, enhancing professional mobility, which is notable for building sustainable careers. Hartung and Di Fabio (2024) argue that career development has entered a fourth paradigm, emphasising that careers should be considered not only in terms of individual success but also in relation to societal well-being and the promotion of decent work. Within this framework, L2 proﬁciency can function as a connective resource that links societies, enhances individuals’ flexibility in the face of precarious working conditions, and strengthens collective awareness, thereby supporting the design of active lives (Guichard, 2022). For the purposes of the current study, however, our focus shifts to approaching the nexus of career development and L2 asset from the opposite perspective. The premise is that as individuals feel competent in pursuing their career and professional growth, they recognise the signiﬁcance of succeeding in L2 to enhance their competitiveness in the global job market by deriving potential beneﬁts from particular personality traits. In other words, self-perceived career competencies, as a professional driving force, could be motivating individuals to attain L2 achievement through the mediating effect of personality attributes, alongside numerous factors and social, psychological, and instructional motives. From such a perspective, we view career competencies as a valuable asset that could influence L2 achievement through a personality trait, namely grit, a social psychological construct linked to academic and career success (Steuber et al., 2019). The existing research has not yet directly examined the integration of the career competen- cies framework with L2 learning within a model. Although career competencies have been exten- sively studied in relation to a range of academic and career-related outcomes (Jo et al., 2024), their role in L2 learning remains largely underexplored. In this study, we intend to examine whether university students’ career competencies would predict their L2 English achievement through the mediating mechanism of language-domain-speciﬁc grit.

## _Grit and achievement_

Grit, characterised as “perseverance and passion for long-term goals” (Duckworth et al., 2007, p. 1087), encompasses the continuous pursuit of objectives, sustaining relentless determination and enthusiasm for an extended duration, despite facing failures, setbacks, or periods of stagnation. Fre- drickson’s (2004) broaden-and-build theory suggests that positive traits, with grit being no excep- tion, contribute to academic success by expanding an individual’s awareness and encouraging exploration, and thus activate cognitive and behavioural processes. Extending the seminal work by Duckworth et al. (2007), which demonstrated the signiﬁcance of grit in different life domains, the number of studies mushroomed to investigate grit in relation to success in academic as well 

BRITISH JOURNAL OF GUIDANCE & COUNSELLING 471

as non-academic settings. The main impetus behind these studies was the conviction that grit plays a pivotal role in determining success (Duckworth, 2017). In the context of educational research, however, the examination of grit has led to diverse results. Carried out across various instructional settings and academic disciplines, some of the studies indicated a relationship between grit and aca- demic outcomes (Bliss & Jacobson, 2020; Calo et al., 2022; Montas et al., 2021), whereas others have presented conflicting results (Dixson, 2021; Steinmayr et al., 2018).

With respect to research on grit within the L2 domain, a recent surge of interest has emerged among scholars. The scholarly attention has primarily focused on exploring the potential associ- ations between L2 learners’ perseverance and passion, termed as L2 grit, which is a domain- speciﬁc conceptualisation (Teimouri et al., 2020), and various L2 outcomes. While doing so, research- ers utilised both domain-general and language domain-speciﬁc grit scales, with the former showing a decreased likelihood of correlating with L2 outcomes (Li & Yang, 2023). Still, whether assessed through domain-general or domain-speciﬁc instruments, a notable collection of studies have demonstrated signiﬁcant associations between L2 grit as a unitary construct and L2 outcomes. These investigations, for instance, have identiﬁed signiﬁcant pathways from grit to L2 achievement (Dehkordi, 2023; Li & Yang, 2023; Liu et al., 2022; Mikami, 2024; Teimouri et al., 2022), L2 proﬁciency (Alrabai, 2022; Hu et al., 2022), and L2 performance (Liu & Wang, 2021; Wei et al., 2019) across diverse contexts. However, within the existing literature, discrepancies emerged when the components of grit, namely perseverance of effort (PoE) and consistency of interest (CoI), were treated as separate factors in predicting L2 outcomes. These inconsistencies manifested in both PoE and CoI showing positive correlations with L2 achievement (Dehkordi et al., 2021), while neither component individu- ally predicted L2 achievement in Khajavy et al. (2020), coupled with a reversal of roles in predictive capacity (Shirvan & Alamer, 2022; Sudina & Plonsky, 2021).

## _Career competencies and grit_

Career competencies (CCs), the ability to shape one’s own career (Akkermans et al., [2013)](#disclosure-statement), encom- pass a broad range of skills and attributes essential for effective career management and advance- ment. Akkermans et al. ([2013)](#disclosure-statement) identiﬁed six career competencies, that is, reflection on motivation, reflection on qualities, networking, self-proﬁling, work exploration, and career control. Likewise, the career development framework by Hillage and Pollard (1998) identiﬁes key competencies such as self-awareness, decision-making, goal setting, and networking as crucial for career pro- gression. Career competencies serve as valuable resources in the journey of career development, providing individuals with essential tools and skills necessary for navigating through the complex- ities of their professional paths (Görgülü & Bozgeyikli, 2024).

Traditionally, research suggests a signiﬁcant overlap between grit, primarily manifesting in the antecedent role, and CCs and career-related outcomes, wherein grit influences career decision- making processes and chosen career paths and goals. Thus, grittier individuals are more likely to engage in long-term objectives and career-related behaviours and functioning (Lee & Sohn, 2017). For example, previous research revealed grits’ relations to career decision self-efficacy (Vela et al., 2018), career success and engagement (Lechner et al., 2019; Walker et al., 2016), career adaptability (Li et al., 2021), career stability (Duckworth & Quinn, 2009), career exploration (Datu et al., 2017), career goals, goal setting and career maturity (Lytle & Shin, 2023; Ting & Datu, 2020), career construc- tion (Zhai et al., 2023), and career satisfaction (Popoola & Karadas, 2022). Moreover, grit served as an effective variable to mediate the links between person-environment ﬁt and career success (Koeke- moer et al., 2023). Additionally, grit stood as a signiﬁcant mediating mechanism to consolidate the association between career-related behaviours, that is, employability attributes such as career agility, resilience and employability competency expectations such as autonomy and personal employability qualities (Ismail et al., 2023).

That being said, in accordance with our study’s framework, prior research also underscores the predictive nature of career-related behaviours, beyond their recognised role as an established 

472 Y. DEMIR ET AL.

outcome variable. To exemplify, in Akkermans et al. ([2018)](#disclosure-statement), career resources such as CCs and career adaptability predicted students’ life satisfaction, study engagement, and academic performance. Like- wise, in Lapan et al. (2016) which involved urban primary school students, engagement with an inte- grated English Language Arts (ELA) and career development curriculum highlighted the signiﬁcance of career agency for students, demonstrating a correlation with essential indicators of ELA proﬁciency such as grades and standardised test scores. In another targeted investigation (Sasaki et al., 2017), it was found that exposure to peers with ambitious career aspirations could elevate students’ motivation to study L2, even in cases where their initial motivation levels are not notably high. Therefore, the present study examines the antecedent role of CCs in a speciﬁc academic domain, namely L2 learning, by testing the mediating role of L2 grit. Building on previous research, it is expected that career com- petencies predict L2 achievement through their positive association with L2 grit.

## _Purpose of the study_

Dedicated to expanding on the empirical base established in earlier works, through a novel, uncharted model of parallel mediation, this study investigates the predictive capacity of CCs in L2 achievement among EFL learners, and the differential mediating functions of L2 grit components (PoE and CoI) in the relationship between CCs and L2 achievement. To achieve these objectives, the following hypotheses were formulated: 

H1: CCs positively predict PoE.

H2: CCs positively predict CoI.

H3: PoE positively predicts L2 achievement.

H4: CoI positively predicts L2 achievement.

H5: CCs indirectly and positively predict L2 achievement through PoE.

H6: CCs indirectly and positively predict L2 achievement through CoI.

# Method

The present study utilised Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) (Kline, 2011; Schumacker & Lomax, 2015). SEM was composed of two models: the Measurement Model and the Structural Model. Measurement models assess the relationships between observed variables and latent constructs, while structural models evaluate the paths among latent constructs. This study employed SEM to explore the parallel mediation roles of PoE and CoI between career competencies (CCs) and L2 achievement.

## _The participants_

The research sample consisted of 290 Turkish university students (206 females and 84 males) enrolled in English preparatory classes of different state universities. In Turkish universities, under- graduate programmes where the language of instruction is English require a year-long English language study, while those conducted with Turkish as the language of instruction offer it as a volun- tary practice before the entry into the programme. A convenience sampling was employed, with the criterion that participants should have spent at least one semester in the English preparatory classes. This made the participants eligible for collecting L2 achievement and L2 grit scores Both a priori and post-hoc power analysis were conducted to determine the appropriate sample size. The a priori analysis suggests that a sample size of 164 participants is adequate to achieve a statistical power of approximately 80% at an alpha level of 0.05, with an RMSEA value of 0.05. The post hoc power was calculated to be greater than 99% based on the RMSEA effect value, degrees

Prior to the study, ethical approval was obtained. The participants were informed about the research purpose which included voluntary participation, and their informed consent was obtained, emphasising that they could withdraw at any time without facing any consequences.

## _Measurements_

The study variables were measured through two quantitative instruments and a personal infor- mation form. We obtained demographic information from the participants including their gender, socio-economic status (SES), and age, as well as their L2 achievement scores.

### _L2 achievement_

In line with Brown et al. (2018) review, we asked the participants to provide the last two English exam scores to measure L2 achievement. All scores were standardised using a 100-point grading system as different scoring systems were used across the participants’ institutions. Then we calculated the mean scores to obtain one particular score reflecting their L2 achievement.

### _Career competencies_

The Career Competencies Questionnaire, originally developed by Akkermans et al. ([2013)](#disclosure-statement) and later validated for a Turkish sample by Görgülü and Bozgeyikli (2024), was employed in this study. This questionnaire assesses six dimensions of career competencies: reflection on motivation (3 items, e.g.: “I know what I like in my work”), reflection on qualities (4 items, e.g.: “I know my strengths in my work”), networking (4 items, e.g.: “I know a lot of people within my work who can help me with my career”), self-proﬁling (3 items, e.g.: “I can clearly show others what my strengthsare in my work”), work exploration (3 items, e.g.: “I know how to ﬁnd out what my options are for becoming further educated”), and career control (4 items, e.g.: “I can make clear career plans”). It comprises 21 items, rated on a 5-point Likert scale. Higher scores indicate greater career competencies. The Dutch sample demonstrated good internal consistency coefficients (Cronbach’s Alpha = .77–.90 across dimensions) and construct validity (Akkermans et al., [2013)](#disclosure-statement). Similarly, the Turkish sample showed good internal consistency coefficients (Cronbach’s Alpha = .86–.94 across dimensions) and construct validity (Görgülü & Bozgeyikli, 2024). The present study found high internal consistency across the dimensions, with omega coefficients ranging from .82 to .89.

### _L2 grit_

This study utilised the language domain-speciﬁc Grit Scale (L2-Grit Scale), developed by Teimouri et al. (2022) and validated for a Turkish sample by Uştuk and Erarslan (2023). The scale measures 

474 Y. DEMIR ET AL.

two dimensions of grit: perseverance of effort (PoE) and consistency of interest (CoI). The scale com- prises 9 items, with ﬁve items for PoE (e.g. “I am a diligent English language learner”) and four reversed-coded items for CoI (e.g. “My interests in learning English change from year to year”), each rated on a ﬁve-point Likert scale. Higher scores in each dimension indicate greater L2- speciﬁc grit. The scale demonstrated sufficient internal consistency (Cronbach’s Alpha = .66–.80 across dimensions and the overall scale) and conﬁrmed construct validity in the original sample (Tei- mouri et al., 2022). On the other hand, the Turkish sample exhibited very good reliability scores (Cronbach’s Alpha = .84–.90 across dimensions and the overall scale) and construct validity (Uştuk & Erarslan, 2023). In this study, the Omega internal consistency coefficients were .87 for PoE and .83 for CoI.

## _Data analysis_

We used the R programming language with RStudio (version 2023.06.1 + 524) for data analysis (RSTUDIO, 2020). Initially, the variables were examined for outliers using z-values. An outlier in L2 achievement (z-value = −3.35) was excluded from the analysis. Additionally, there were only 8 missing values in L2 achievement, which were addressed using the listwise deletion method. To describe the data, we utilised the “psych” (Revelle, 2024) and “dplyr” (Wickham et al., 2024) packages. In this study, Herman’s one factor test was applied to assess whether the results were affected using a single data collection method (e.g. self-reported measures), commonly referred to as common method bias (Fuller et al., 2015; Podsakoff et al., 2003). This test calculates the proportion of variance in the model’s variables that can be attributed to a single factor. If the variance explained by a single factor exceeds 50%, it indicates a common factor influenced the analysis. The analysis showed that the ﬁrst unrotated factor explained 37.76% of the variance. These ﬁndings provide evidence that common method bias is not a signiﬁcant concern in this study. For the main analysis, which involved Structural Equation Modeling (SEM), we employed the “lavaan” package (Rosseel, 2024) and “semPlot” package (Epskamp, 2015).

In the SEM analysis, latent variables included CCs, PoE, and CoI, while observed variables con- sisted of the items for PoE and CoI, the total scores for the dimensions of CCs (reflection on motivation, reflection on qualities, networking, self-proﬁling, work exploration, and career control), and L2 achievement. In this study, parcelling was employed to represent the latent vari- able CCs through aggregated scores of its dimensions. Item parcelling, commonly utilised in factor analysis and structural equation modelling (SEM), entails aggregating multiple items into a single composite indicator. This method has both advantages (such as reduce model complex- ity) and disadvantages (such as bias), therefore it should be used carefully (Little et al., 2013). In this study, this decision was based on several methodological and theoretical considerations. Firstly, the dimensions of CCs can theoretically be argued to demonstrate homogeneity in their content. Methodologically, the second-order CFA analysis supports construct validity and demon- strates the holistic structure of CCs. A second-order CFA was conducted to verify the strength of the relationships between the dimensions and the higher-order factor (CCs). The second-order CFA model demonstrated an acceptable ﬁt to the data (CFI = 0.93, TLI = 0.92, RMSEA = 0.079, SRMR = 0.048). The factor loadings for both ﬁrst-order factors (dimensions) and especially the second-order factor (CCs) were signiﬁcant (_p_ \< 0.001) and generally high (\>0.7 standardised). These ﬁndings suggest that the CCs’ dimensions are well-represented and theoretically coherent. Given these considerations, item parcelling can be a justiﬁed approach to reduce measurement error, enhance model stability, and improve the ﬁt of our complex model with a relatively small sample size (Little et al., 2013).

SEM was conducted through the following steps: model speciﬁcation, model identiﬁcation, model estimation, model testing, and model modiﬁcation (Schumacker & Lomax, 2015). The model was speciﬁed and identiﬁed based on the conceptual framework outlined in the literature section. A bootstrapping method with robust maximum likelihood estimation was used for model 

BRITISH JOURNAL OF GUIDANCE & COUNSELLING 475

estimation. Initially, the measurement model estimations conﬁrmed that all factor loadings were sig- niﬁcant. Subsequently, model ﬁt indices were examined. We used Chi-square, CFI, TLI, RMSEA, and SRMR as ﬁt indices. Although Chi-square is ideally expected to be insigniﬁcant, it tends to be signiﬁ- cant with larger sample sizes. Therefore, we relied on other indices to complement the Chi-square. For a good model ﬁt, CFI and TLI values should be .90 or above, while RMSEA and SRMR values should be below .08. (Schumacker & Lomax, 2015). After evaluating the path coefficients, the results were reported.

# Results

Table 2 present the correlations among variables, internal consistency (omega) and AVE (average variance extracted) coefficients. It is remarkable that correlations between career competencies and CoI were weak or insigniﬁcant.

To test the hypotheses, SEM was conducted as shown in Figure 1. Before examining the full SEM model, the measurement model was conﬁrmed. Table 3 shows that all factor loadings of the measurement model were signiﬁcant and had acceptable magnitudes.

Full SEM model tested and after two modiﬁcations on PoE, model ﬁt indices were as shown: Chi- square = 296.75, df = 142, _p_ \< .001, CFI = .95, TLI = .93, RMSEA = 0.062, 90% CI\[0.052, 0.072\], SRMR = 0.063. Model ﬁt indices show that the data were suitable for suggested theorical model sufficiently. Figure 1 shows that CCs signiﬁcantly predicted PoE (_b_ = 0.61, SE = 0.07) but did not predict CoI (_b_ = 0.05, SE = 0.04). Therefore, H1 was supported while H2 was not. L2 achievement had only direct relationships with PoE (_b_ = 3.22, SE = 1.27), conﬁrming H3 but not H4. Finally, the indirect relationships were signiﬁcant for the mediating role of PoE (_b_ = 1.97, SE = 0.85). PoE mediated the relationships between CCs and L2 achievement, supporting H5. This means that higher CCs can predict L2 achievement by increasing PoE. However, this indirect relationship was not signiﬁ- cant for CoI (_b_ = 0.11, SE = 0.14), so H6 is not supported. Table 4 shows the direct, indirect, and total relationships.

# Discussion

In the globalised business world, proﬁciency in L2 can be a critical requirement. Consequently, careers serve as a motivator for the development of L2 skills among individuals. In line with this, our study demonstrates that career competencies (CCs) were indirectly linked to L2 achievement through perseverance of effort (PoE). Firstly, CCs positively predicted PoE. These competencies com- prise components such as awareness of one’s own skills and goals, the capability to set and plan career goals, and these components can motivate individuals to persist in their efforts to achieve L2 proﬁciency. Therefore, career competencies may function as motivational factors that facilitate sustained effort in L2 learning, similar to career aspirations (Sasaki et al., 2017) and career-oriented curricula (Lapan et al., 2016). According to Morris’ (2011) study, determining career goals, a com- ponent of career control, was a signiﬁcant motivator for language learning. Furthermore, Akkermans et al. ([2018)](#disclosure-statement) suggested that career competencies can initiate motivational processes as valuable resources. Additionally, the relationship between competencies and grit is not conﬁned to career contexts. Wei et al. (2020) found that self-related L2 competencies predicted L2 grit, indicating that as individuals’ conﬁdence in their own competencies increases, they may exhibit greater deter- mination to succeed.

In this study, PoE also positively predicted L2 achievement. The relationship between PoE and L2 achievement has been observed in numerous studies in the literature (Alamer, [2021;](#disclosure-statement) Datu et al., 2017; Shirvan & Alamer, 2022; Teimouri et al., 2020). These studies suggested that PoE, as opposed to CoI, can predict academic outcomes regardless of cultural differences. Credé et al. (2017) also emphasises the importance of maintaining consistent effort and diligence to successfully complete the tasks necessary for achieving one’s goals. (PoE) is closely related to achievement, as it involves consistently maintaining effort and dedication over time to accomplish one’s goals. However, Sudina and Plonsky’s (2021) study contradicts this ﬁnding, as PoE did not signiﬁcantly predict l2 achievement. They construed this discrepancy as unsurprising since the students in their sample attended language classes voluntarily and might not have had any career or other advantages associated with this learning activity. As previously mentioned, English language proﬁciency is essential for career-related goals in Türkiye and other non-English-speaking countries. Therefore, PoE could be considered as a signiﬁcant driving force

in situations where L2 learning is perceived as a necessity or requirement, especially in the context of developing countries.

On the other hand, CoI was not found to be associated with either career competencies or L2 achievement. Demir (2024) stated that the relationship between CoI and L2-related variables varied across studies, making it a contentious dimension. There were several explanations for this discrepancy. Some researchers suggest revisiting the deﬁnition of the construct (Credé et al., 2017; Shirvan & Alamer, 2022). Another rationale leaned on cultural differences (Demir, 2024; Datu et al., 2017). Datu et al. (2017) noted that CoI might not have signiﬁcant meaning for achiev- ing academic goals in collectivist cultures. In such cultures, meeting the expectations of others might be more important than maintaining one’s own passion. Therefore, gritty individuals in col- lectivist societies may not necessarily need to sustain their interest in L2 to achieve academic success. Supporting this inference, while CoI was found to be a signiﬁcant predictor of success in a study conducted in the United States setting (Sudina & Plonsky, 2021), it did not predict achievement in studies conducted among Saudi and Iranian samples (Alamer, [2021;](#disclosure-statement) Shirvan & Alamer, 2022; Teimouri et al., 2020). The speciﬁc result of the present study can also be viewed in this light, considering the Turkish context, which, while being a rich and diverse mosaic that resists easy classiﬁcation on the collectivist/individualist scale, generally exhibits collectivist incli- nations (Göregenli, 1997).

This insight becomes more meaningful in relation to career situations. Career competencies did not predict CoI. This could be because, for the Turkish youth, career competencies and university life are linked to extrinsic goals, such as obtaining a profession. A study investigating the reasons why Turkish youth attend university found that vocational goals were prominent (Görgülü et al., 2025). Additionally, Türkiye also implements an examination-based selection and placement system for the transition from middle school to high school, through university. This system encourages young people to study regularly starting from early ages, with hard work being highly valued. For example, students must cover and solve problems and questions in various ﬁelds such as maths, physics, and geography, even if they are not interested, to achieve higher scores. Therefore, the CoI dimension might be irrelevant and have limited functionality in certain cultures and conditions. This study found a relationship between career competencies and L2 achievement, albeit an indir- ect one. We interpret this result within the context of the Turkish labour market, suggesting that Turkish students might strive for L2 achievement due to employment pressures, rather than out of a genuine passion for learning L2. Students with higher career competencies might be more cog- nizant of the relationship between career choice and L2 achievement. They might feel the need to work hard to promote and increase their career opportunities, which drives them to persist in their efforts. As a result, this persistence ultimately leads to higher L2 achievement scores. In this view, passion for L2, that is, consistency of interest, may not have a game-changing role for CCs or L2 achievement. We can observe that this is also probably due to the labour market in Türkiye with high unemployment rates (Turkish Statistical Institute, 2024). With high unemployment in Türkiye, young individuals may feel compelled to view L2 learning as a practical requirement for securing employment rather than as an intrinsic interest or personal enthusiasm.

BRITISH JOURNAL OF GUIDANCE & COUNSELLING 479

This pattern can also be interpreted within the expectancy–value framework (Wigﬁeld & Eccles, 2000). From this perspective, the psychological mechanism underlying these relationships may be associated with the task value students attribute to L2 learning. As career competencies increase, students may assign greater importance to L2 learning, particularly in terms of attainment and utility values, for the reasons discussed above. This increase in perceived task value may, in turn, lead to greater effort investment and higher achievement. Although the other core component of the framework – students’ expectancy for success – was not examined in the present study, future research could extend the model by incorporating perceived competence or self-efficacy.

## _Implications_

Given that career competencies indirectly enhance L2 achievement through perseverance, there are potential implications. In line with United Nations Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 4 access to inclusive and equitable quality education is essential for sustainable human development (United Nations, 2015). From a sustainability science perspective (Komiyama & Takeuchi, 2006; Sahle et al., 2025; Takeuchi et al., 2017), education also plays an important role in in promoting this perspective. In the context of the present study, higher education institutions should consider L2 learning as part of sustainable human development, and academic units should collaborate for these broader goals. Speciﬁcally, schools of foreign languages may develop joint programmes with career centres. In this way, students can understand the importance of L2 learning for career sustainability by developing career competencies early on. Introducing career competency training from the ﬁrst year of univer- sity, especially in preparatory language programmes, may positively influence academic success in L2 learning. Therefore, it would be beneﬁcial for higher educational institutions to consider integrat- ing brief, group-based career counselling programmes into their preparatory language programmes. Career counsellors in career centres can work with students in preparatory language programmes to raise awareness of the importance of L2 for their future career trajectories.

In addition to integrating career counselling into L2 learning, career counselling interventions themselves could be conducted in the L2, thereby simultaneously supporting students’ language development and enhancing their career competencies. This could entail incorporating career plan- ning workshops, goal-setting exercises, and skill awareness sessions conducted in the L2 used within the language curriculum. It is also recommended to increase efforts both within and outside the cur- riculum to facilitate the acquisition of career skills. Although this research focuses solely on L2 achievement, other studies (e.g. Akkermans et al., [2018)](#disclosure-statement) have shown that career competencies can be a signiﬁcant predictor across various academic outcomes.

The ﬁndings of the study indicate that the role of consistency of interest and persistence of inter- est in L2 achievement may differ across different cultural contexts. Consequently, it is essential for educators and policymakers to consider cultural factors when designing language programmes with career-related content. For instance, in collectivist cultures where extrinsic goals and societal expectations may be salient, language programmes may beneﬁt from emphasising the practical and career-related beneﬁts of L2 proﬁciency.

## _Limitations and future research_

Considering the scarcity of research that simultaneously explores L2 achievement and career development, this study represents a novel and valuable contribution to the ﬁeld. However, this study also has certain limitations. Since this study adopts a cross-sectional design, it is difficult to draw deﬁnitive conclusions about causality. Longitudinal studies would better capture the development of these relationships over time. Additionally, longitudinal studies could contribute to understanding the reciprocal and recursive relationships between career competencies, L2 grit, and achievement. Secondly, other potential individual difference variables that could impact the relationships of PoE, CoI, and L2 achievement were not included. For instance, factors such as 

480 Y. DEMIR ET AL.

individuals’ socio-economic status, family backgrounds, or educational history should also be taken into account. Furthermore, the sample in this study consisted of preparatory English stu- dents at universities, neglecting L2 learners in different contexts (e.g. elective courses, high school level, private courses, etc.). Given that many preparatory classes are mandatory, the results should be interpreted speciﬁcally within this context.

Additionally, future research should explore grit in English language learning across various cul- tures. Academic and career-related variables are thought to be important for understanding the factors that drive L2 learning. These variables are susceptible to the influences of culture and the present labour market. Therefore, comparative studies between Western and Eastern settings, as well as countries with varying economic conditions, could provide a better understanding of these relationships. Given the mixed ﬁndings on CoI in the literature, it is also recommended that future research should address alternative deﬁnitions and measures of CoI. This could help clarify its role and improve the consistency of ﬁndings across studies.

# Notes on contributors

***Yusuf Demir*** works as a professor at Selçuk University, Department of English Language Education. His research focuses on second language teacher education, oral corrective feedback, the use of emerging technologies in language teach- ing, and L2 grit. He has published widely in these areas and continues to explore innovative approaches to improving L2 learning and instruction.

***Zeynep Görgülü*** is a PhD candidate in Guidance and Psychological Counseling at Ankara University and works as a research assistant at Selçuk University in the same department. Her research interests focus on career counseling, with a particular emphasis on career transitions, school-to-work transition, university students’ career development, and career competencies.

***Hasan Bozgeyikli*** works as a professor in the Department of Guidance and Psychological Counseling at Selçuk Univer- sity. His primary research interests include career counseling and university students’ career development. In addition to his work in these areas, he also conducts research in school counseling and broader topics within educational sciences.
